title: Anemia of Inflammation: Find the Driver and the Overlap
bottomLine: Anemia of inflammation is usually a consequence of an identifiable chronic inflammatory, infectious, malignant or organ disease process. Diagnose the pattern in context, look actively for concurrent iron deficiency or CKD, and treat the underlying disease; erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy belongs to selected disease-specific pathways rather than routine primary-care treatment of every inflammatory anemia.
recognize: The anemia is commonly normocytic but can become mildly microcytic; reticulocyte response is often inappropriately low for the degree of anemia.
Ferritin may be normal or elevated because it is an acute-phase reactant, so a seemingly reassuring ferritin does not automatically exclude concurrent iron deficiency.
differentiate: Differentiate isolated inflammation-related anemia from true iron deficiency, CKD anemia, marrow disease, hemolysis, nutritional deficiency and mixed anemia; multimorbidity frequently produces more than one mechanism.
Low serum iron is not specific for iron deficiency: iron sequestration during inflammation can lower circulating iron while total stores are preserved or increased.
assessment: Define the chronic disease burden and inflammatory activity, bleeding risk, renal function, nutrition, medications, malignancy/infection symptoms and prior CBC/iron trends.
Assess functional impact and urgent anemia symptoms such as syncope, ischemic chest discomfort, severe dyspnea or hemodynamic compromise rather than grading urgency from hemoglobin alone.
workup: Use CBC, reticulocyte count and ferritin as part of the anemia evaluation; add transferrin saturation/iron studies when inflammation or CKD makes ferritin difficult to interpret or concurrent deficiency is suspected.

Investigate unexplained or disproportionate anemia rather than labeling it 'chronic disease' simply because the patient has a chronic diagnosis; cytopenias, abnormal smear findings or rapid progression may require hematology evaluation.
management: Treat and optimize the underlying inflammatory/infectious/malignant condition and replace proven nutritional or iron deficiency when present.

For CKD-associated anemia, use the current KDIGO anemia-in-CKD pathway for iron, ESA, HIF-PHI and transfusion decisions; treatment is individualized to symptoms, CKD stage, cardiovascular/thrombotic risk and patient preferences.
Transfusion decisions are driven by clinical instability, active bleeding, symptoms and the treatment context rather than a single universal outpatient hemoglobin trigger.
medicationSafety: Do not start an ESA solely because hemoglobin is low in a patient with inflammation; ESAs have disease-specific indications and thrombotic/cardiovascular risks.

Avoid giving iron indefinitely when iron deficiency has not been demonstrated; conversely, inflammation can mask true deficiency, so do not dismiss iron deficiency from ferritin alone when the clinical context is suspicious.
redFlags: Rapidly worsening anemia or new pancytopenia
Abnormal smear/blasts or constitutional symptoms suggesting marrow disease or malignancy
Hemodynamic instability, active bleeding or ischemic symptoms
ESA hyporesponsiveness or complex CKD anemia requiring nephrology/hematology input
counselling: Explain that the anemia is often linked to the underlying disease and may improve as that disease is controlled.
Clarify why treatment may focus on inflammation, kidney disease or iron deficiency rather than automatically prescribing iron or a red-cell stimulating drug.
followUp: Trend CBC and disease activity at an interval matched to severity and the treatment plan.
Revisit the diagnosis if anemia progresses despite improved disease control or if new cytopenias, bleeding, renal decline or nutritional risk develops.
examTrap: Seeing chronic inflammation and a low hemoglobin and immediately prescribing iron or an ESA without confirming the anemia mechanism and checking for CKD, blood loss or marrow disease.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory anemia is a context diagnosis; treat the driver and look for a second cause hiding underneath.

title: Macrocytic Anemia: Classify the Pattern Before Treating It
bottomLine: Macrocytosis is a pattern, not a diagnosis. Separate megaloblastic from non-megaloblastic causes using the history, smear and reticulocyte response, then evaluate B12, alcohol/liver disease, thyroid disease, medications, reticulocytosis and marrow disorders; neurologic B12 deficiency requires prompt treatment even if the CBC is not dramatically abnormal.
recognize: Macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils support megaloblastic physiology, while round macrocytes or isolated macrocytosis can occur with alcohol, liver disease, medications or other non-megaloblastic causes.
Reticulocytosis after hemolysis or blood loss can increase MCV because reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells.
differentiate: B12 deficiency can produce neurologic injury; folate deficiency does not explain the same posterior-column/myeloneuropathy pattern.

Unexplained macrocytosis with multiple cytopenias, dysplastic cells or progressive counts raises concern for myelodysplastic syndrome or another marrow disorder rather than a simple vitamin deficiency.
assessment: Review neurologic symptoms, alcohol use, diet, GI surgery/malabsorption, medications, hypothyroid symptoms, liver disease, bleeding/hemolysis clues and pregnancy status.
Perform a neurologic examination when B12 deficiency is possible and assess for hepatosplenomegaly, bleeding/infection signs or other evidence of marrow disease.
workup: Use CBC with smear and reticulocyte count to define the pattern; order B12 when clinically indicated and use the current laboratory algorithm rather than a universal cutoff.

Assess thyroid/liver testing and hemolysis markers when suggested by the history and smear; folate testing is rarely required in contemporary Canadian practice and may require laboratory consultation in some jurisdictions.
Refer for marrow evaluation when persistent unexplained macrocytosis is accompanied by cytopenias or dysplasia after common reversible causes are addressed.
management: Treat the cause: replace B12 promptly when deficiency is clinically important, supplement folate when indicated while protecting against untreated B12 deficiency, address alcohol/medication contributors and treat thyroid/liver disease appropriately.
Do not delay treatment of neurologic B12 deficiency while waiting for the MCV to become abnormal or for every secondary test to return.
medicationSafety: Folic acid alone can improve the blood count while clinically important B12-related neurologic injury remains untreated; replace B12 when deficiency is plausible or confirmed.
Review medications associated with macrocytosis before ordering invasive testing, but do not attribute progressive cytopenias to medication without a defensible evaluation.
redFlags: Progressive gait abnormality, objective neuropathy or cognitive change with possible B12 deficiency
Hemodynamic instability or severe symptomatic anemia
counselling: Explain that a large red-cell size is a clue requiring a cause, not a disease name by itself.
Patients with permanent B12 malabsorption need an ongoing replacement plan; patients with alcohol- or medication-related macrocytosis need the causal risk addressed rather than repeated CBCs alone.
followUp: Confirm clinical and CBC response after correcting the identified cause and reassess if MCV/cytopenias persist.
Neurologic recovery from B12 deficiency can lag behind hematologic improvement and requires symptom-focused follow-up.
examTrap: Treating every high MCV with folate before checking B12 risk/neurologic findings—or assuming a normal hemoglobin rules out clinically important B12 deficiency.
oneLinePearl: Macrocytosis asks two questions first: megaloblastic or not, and is B12-related neurologic injury being missed?
sourceBasis: BC Guidelines — Cobalamin (Vitamin B12) and Folate Deficiency (2023)
